speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first of all I wish to thank the hon. member for his kind words. I will not elaborate further on my own respect for his views and his abilities because of my fear that after ten o'clock this House might turn into a mutual admiration society.
He has mentioned areas of disagreement in terms of policies in this field, particularly on the question of universality versus selectivity. It is indeed my considered view that while we should retain the element of universality in old age pensions with basic old age pensions, we also must have a supplement which will help those people who really need to be helped. I am supported in this respect by all provincial governments in the practice they have followed, including governments belonging to the party of my hon. friend. Not one single NDP government at the provincial level has increased the basic old age pension, while some of them have not hesitated to increase the supplement. I can understand that rationale very well.
The hon. member also talks about means tests. I wish I could convince him that what we are talking about here is an income test. I think he has been used to the criteria in the previous legislation, but we have moved to an income test and there is a significant difference between them. I suspect we will have an opportunity to discuss that later.
It is true that the last budget helped senior citizens, particularly those over the guaranteed income supplement rate. 1 must stress, however, that senior citizens with marginal incomes apart from what they could get if they are on a partial guaranteed income supplement, will also benefit from the provisions contained in the budget. This should not be ignored particularly in relation to the $1,000 exemption for senior citizens on private pension plans.
The hon. member argues that we should now add to the basic and guaranteed income supplement. I can only tell him that we have made a lot of progress in the last three years. I have no time tonight to go over that, but I will indicate that we will again have escalation on January 1 which will bring the OAS/GIS benefits to over $200 a month.
After Christmas I hope to introduce a bill that will provide income tested benefits to spouses between ages 60 and 65. So we are making progress, though maybe not as

fast as the hon. member would wish. I understand his eagerness; he has been an eager beaver, if I may say so, in this area for many, many years and has been prodding successive governments in this field. I respect his views but I am telling him we are making progress.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my appearance on the late show debate comes as a result of my question to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) on October 22 regarding limited dividend housing, which is a program extremely vital to my district.

Having regard for limited dividend housing, the main city in my district, the city of Cornerbrook, with the complete support of funding from the province is providing a regional college to look after some 500 students who will come from all parts of the west coast, and require low cost housing, but also will require accommodation for some 50 to 100 professors and their families. This, naturally, will require housing development, along with many other public services for additional citizens and children.
It is obvious then that the federal government must treat as a priority the need to provide this housing, in co-operation with the provincial government and private entrepreneurs.
This focuses attention on the flexibility of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to rise to the task, along with the government of Canada, to provide the funds and to induce contractors to enter this field and fill the need in Newfoundland and the Atlantic region generally. I point out the need to support progress, even though existing limited dividend housing in areas which already exist leave much to be desired. In referring to low cost rental housing it is obvious that the greatest need in Canada is in the field of low rental public housing for those on fixed incomes and for those having to resort to welfare.
Unfortunately, public housing has gone beyond the comprehension of the ability of provincial governments to cope with the cost. May I again use my own province as an example. Under the Newfoundland and Labrador Housing Corporation public housing is gone beyond their financial capability to cope when recent tenders have indicated that the lowest tenders offered were in the area of $45,000 per row house unit. This puts a complete block into the capability of the province and it emphasizes the need for alternative sources of housing.

It has become recognized, Mr. Speaker, if I may deal with this area of concern, that the most economical type of home which can be provided is the mobile type of home, or the prefabricated home and it is my opinion that this is the area that should be explored to try to answer the short term problem of housing.

If we all do our duty then we, as a parliament, will be performing our duty in serving the needs of our population.

IMMIGRATION-POSSIBLE INCREASE IN NUMBER OF CHILEAN REFUGEES ADMITTED-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I rise to plead for more Canadian compassion for the many political victims and prisoners in Chile, I wish to put my remarks in the larger context of the violation of human rights sweeping the world.
Only today Amnesty International, a world-wide organization of individuals working to end political terrorism and torture, met with members of Parliament from all parties. We learned of their efforts to end torture-inflicted by governments-in the more than 30 countries where Amnesty International has affirmed the use of torture as a political instrument.
There is a new characteristic in this torture. It is used not only to obtain information but to control dissident elements in dictatorial and repressive regimes.
The World Conference of Religion for Peace, which convened recently in Belgium, has provided the same information as Amnesty International. There have been massacres and tortures in Northern Ireland, the Philippines, the Middle East and Cyprus, as well as Viet Nam and Cambodia. The escalation of violence and the continuing violation of human rights in the world led the World Conference of Religion for Peace to urge governments to construct policies "that will hold inviolate the spirit of man, and guarantee his physical and cultural wellbeing." For peace is incompatible with the violation of basic human rights.
This brings us to Chile, a country with a long democratic tradition suppressed by a four-man military junta whose continued authority lies in force. Chileans by the thousands have tried to escape from their country since the coup in September, 1973 which was followed by waves of persecution-not because they are criminals but because they oppose the draconian authoritarianism of the junta. The repression, imprisonments and tortures have become so bad that the United Nations has passed a
November 28, 1974

special resolution calling on Chile to respect fundamental freedom.
On October 9, 1974, a group of 24 distinguished Canadians, representing a cross-section of leadership in the churches, labour and education, came to Parliament Hill and presented a brief to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras). This brief claimed that Canadian policy toward Chile has been inadequate to the human emergency, and that Canadian concern for the ideals of the United Nations and for social justice has not been borne out by Canadian government actions.
Specifically, the brief said that Canada had been virtually silent regarding the extinction of democratic institutions in Chile, the systematic reign of terror, the mockery of justice and brutality which has characterized the rule of the junta.
With regard to economic relations the brief charged that Canada had collaborated with multilateral organizations dominated by the United States to extend economic assistance to the junta. Canadian government institutions and Canadian business have co-operated to promote Canadian investment in Chile.
With regard to immigration, the brief charged that Canada has acted reluctantly and slowly in the refugee situation created by the coup. Only 955 Chileans were admitted to Canada in the first six months of 1974, fewer people than were admitted from Ecuador. The 955 compares with 184 for the first six months of 1973, but barely scratches the surface of this new problem. Expressed humanitarian concern by the Canadian government has been contradicted by lengthy processes and excessive security interrogations, the brief claims.
The lengthy brief and 14 recommendations, chief of which was that the government broaden its Chilean refugee program to allow 10,000 persons to enter Canada under the immigration refugee category. This special category would include people in prisons and concentration camps, those who are harassed by authorities, and those who have reached temporary shelter in third countries such as Panama, Peru and Argentina.
On October 22 I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration what response he would make to these recommendations. To this date there has been no response. But the Canadian Council of Churches, as one of the participants in the brief, has received a response from the office of the external affairs minister. It is this response that concerns me greatly and is the reason I have taken the floor tonight. For the external affairs department says the situation in Chile is normalizing and, moreover, that our support of the UN resolution demonstrates our concern for human rights in Chile.
But the situation in Chile is not normalizing, Mr. Speaker; it is getting worse. Secret trials in the Chilean navy are taking place, with the death penalty being sought. The Italian and Columbian embassies are being besieged with new refugees. Mexico has just broken relations with Chile. Not content with the 2,500 Chileans who have died violent deaths since the coup, the junta is tightening its grip. The World Council of Churches has just cabled its Canadian
Adjournment Debate
office to step up its support of interchurch work in Chile and Argentina, now coping with waves of arrests of ordinary workers and farmers. The World Council now estimates that there are 100,000 Chilean refugees in Argentina, 15,000 of whom are registered, which is a 50 per cent increase in the past few months.
All of this should be of great concern to the Canadian government which could provide more help than just support of a UN resolution. If we are not going to reappraise our economic relations with Chile so that we get out of the invidious position of supporting repression, could we not at least open our doors a bit wider? The Chilean government has offered to release political prisoners who have a country to go to. Surely our response can be a bit better than the assurance of the immigration minister that Canada's special immigration office in Santiago will remain open. The brief presented to the government goes much deeper into the problem and requires a better response than the minister's bland assurance that applications from refugees will be processed.
I have met some of the Chileans who have fled to Canada. They are professional, and middle class and labour people whose only crime was that they wanted to be free. Certainly, strict security measures must be enforced-and they are. In one group of 12,165 Chilean applicants, only 45 were rejected for security reasons, but very few of the others were admitted to Canada.
We should rid our minds of the idea that the Chilean refugees are communists or Marxists. Just because the slain Salvadore Allende headed a Marxist regime, it does not make all Chileans ideological communists. As the Rev. John Zimmerman, executive secretary of the Lutheran Council of Canada, noted when he came to Parliament Hill with the delegation, these people would, if they lived in Canada, be ordinary members of labour groups. They are certainly no more dangerous to Canadian life than the Hungarians, Czechs and Ugandans that Canada took in during their time of ordeal.
Canada has a well-deserved reputation for compassion. We have an economically and socially strong society to back up that reputation. Today another group of oppressed people, the Chileans, look to us for help.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: IMMIGRATION-POSSIBLE INCREASE IN NUMBER OF CHILEAN REFUGEES ADMITTED-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to answer the hon. member on behalf of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), who could not be here tonight. First of all may I say that Canada's effort was among the most active of any of the countries which established processing facilities in Chile to admit refugees for permanent resettlement, as is evidenced by the large number of persons authorized to come to Canada. Our effort in this case has been based on humanitarian considerations.
With particular reference to the brief referred to by the hon. member, presented a short while ago by the Canadian Council of Churches and other organizations to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, their recommendations are being reviewed and a reply will be sent to them shortly.
However, I should like to put on the record the fact that, following the coup in Chile last September, the Department of Manpower and Immigration immediately estab-

November 28, 1974
Adjournment Debate
lished a full processing capacity in Santiago. Because of this special effort it was possible to process applications in an expeditious manner and to meet deadlines as they arose. Although normal immigration, medical and background checks are, of course, continued even in movements of this kind, the norms of assessment were relaxed as they have been in other such similar situations. In addition, special concessions were made by allowing some people to come forward before their examinations were completed rather than risk the possible consequences of further delay.
Departmental officers worked in close co-operation with representatives of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, as well as other interested groups in making known the Canadian government's willingness to accept refugees, and our officials visited persons in camps in various countries to conduct interviews. During January, 1974, an armed forced aircraft on a training flight was diverted to Santiago when commercial services proved inadequate to move people quickly enough to safety, and 170 persons arrived on the flight.
To date, Mr. Speaker, applications have been received from about 4,000 Chileans who come within the United Nations definition of "refugee". Of these, more than 1,500
have been authorized to enter Canada, and more than 850 have already arrived as immigrants. About 750 have withdrawn their applications, and slightly more than 550 have been refused because of adverse background or character reports, or because they could not meet even the relaxed selection criteria used to assess the likelihood that they could successfully settle in Canada-for example, total illiteracy. About 1,150 are still in process.
The full range of services normally extended to refugees, such as transportation assistance, language training, employment counselling and placement, and, in emergency situations, financial aid, is available to these people.
One question that has been asked from time to time is that, if over 2,700 persons from Chile have been authorized to enter Canada since September, 1973, why have only 1,250 done so? There is of course more than one answer to this question, but such things as acceptance by another preferred country or a change of heart would probably account for most of these cases.
